Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) excel academ-
ically but struggle with social intelligence tasks,
such as creating good compromises. In this
paper, we present methods for generating em-
pathically neutral compromises between two
opposing viewpoints. We first compared four
different prompt engineering methods using
Claude 3 Opus and a dataset of 2,400 contrast-
ing views on shared places. A subset of the gen-
erated compromises was evaluated for accept-
ability in a 50-participant study. We found that
the best method for generating compromises
between two views used external empathic sim-
ilarity between a compromise and each view-
point as iterative feedback, outperforming stan-
dard Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning. The
results indicate that the use of empathic neutral-
ity improves the acceptability of compromises.
The dataset of generated compromises was then
used to train two smaller foundation models via
margin-based alignment of human preferences,
improving efficiency and removing the need for
empathy estimation during inference.
1
Introduction
Living in liberal, plural societies requires compro-
mise and consensus. While these two components
are essential for healthy deliberation and decision-
making, they are not the same. For example, while
multiple parties in one household could prefer dif-
ferent types of meat for dinner (e.g., chicken, beef,
lamb), they might come to a consensus that they all
want meat for dinner, but they may also compro-
mise by agreeing to delay eating beef and lamb for
another time and eating chicken tonight, because
there is only chicken in the refrigerator.

Recent research shows that LLMs can promote
democratic deliberation by fostering consensus (de-
veloping statements different participants can agree
on) and reducing polarization, often outperform-
ing human mediators in clarity and inclusiveness
(Tessler et al., 2024). Additionally, Bakker et al.
(2022) show that fine-tuning LLMs to generate con-
sensus statements from diverse individual prefer-
ences enhances group acceptance of the statements
more efficiently than traditional negotiation pro-
cesses.
However, these examples concern using LLMs
to develop consensus statements across broad view-
points. Developing compromises between different
and opposing viewpoints, on the other hand, re-
quires a greater degree of social intelligence that
LLMs may lack (Xu et al., 2024). Although LLMs
can produce empathetic responses (Welivita et al.,
2021; Sabour et al., 2022; Majumder et al., 2020)
and can generate consensus statements, they have
not been used to generate neutral compromises.
Generating compromises are fundamentally differ-
ent, as successful compromises (i.e., acceptable
to both parties) require proposing resolutions that
make both parties better off compared to in the ab-
sence of any compromise (Van Parijs, 2012). This
thus requires attending to a solution space that al-
lows for differing viewpoints to both find positives
compared to their original stances. Recent stud-
ies show that while LLMs can analyze disputes
and generate intervention messages, their effective-
ness as neutral mediators remain inconsistent (Tan
et al., 2024). Similar concerns arise in humani-
tarian frontline negotiations, where neutrality and
sensitivity are critical. Interviews with practition-
ers highlighted that, although LLMs can synthesize
large amounts of information, they may be biased,

which can lead to mixed outcomes when supporting
neutral negotiation processes (Ma et al., 2024).
Inspired by these earlier works, this paper ex-
plores whether LLMs can generate neutral compro-
mises for contrasting views (i.e., generate compro-
mises that do not favor either view). This ability
would be valuable in scenarios where impartiality
is crucial, such as collaborative decision-making
and conflict resolution. Particularly, we investigate
the following research questions:
RQ1: Can prompt engineering be used to generate
compromises that are empathically neutral between
two diverse viewpoints (about a place)?
RQ2: Can smaller, open-source LLMs replicate
empathically neutral compromise generation capa-
bilities based on a larger, proprietary model, and
remove the need for explicit empathy estimation
during inference?
To address these questions, we propose a task
that focuses on generating compromises from a
pair of contrasting views (Figure 1). As a first ex-
ploration of this task, we use pairs of contrasting
positive and negative viewpoints about safety and
welcomingness of public spaces from Chen et al.
(2025). The positive views (view_A) are about feel-
ing either safe or welcome and the negative views
(view_B) are about feeling less safe or excluded.
Each viewpoint includes a participant’s proposal
for improving the safety or welcomingness of a
place. In our task, generated compromises for im-
proving safety or welcomingness between a pair
of positive and negative views should: (i) consider
both suggestions and (ii) be empathically neutral.
Since greater empathy helps people to understand
each other’s opinions and viewpoints, empathy is
important to compromise, which requires conces-
sions from the parties involved. While individual
parties agree to a compromise because they would
be worse off without it (Van Parijs, 2012), if two
views are judged to be similarly empathetic towards
a compromise, or empathically neutral, the prob-
ability of finding a suggested compromise accept-
able should naturally increase.
To address RQ1, we explore several prompt-
based controls to guide the generation process. We
investigated guiding the model toward empathic
neutrality by providing explicit feedback on the
empathic similarity (Shen, 2023) between each of
the two views and the generated compromise (Sec-
tion 3.2). When the empathic similarity scores
across both views are balanced, the generated com-
promise is considered empathically neutral. A 50-
participant human evaluation of a subset of the
compromises was conducted to assess the accept-
ability of the different compromise generation ap-
proaches and showed that compromises generated
by the model informed with empathic neutrality
was highly preferred.
To address RQ2, we use the compromises gener-
ated in RQ1 to explore an alignment technique to
teach empathetically neutral compromise genera-
tion abilities to smaller, pretrained language mod-
els (Liu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024) Motivated
by how humans internalize social norms not just by
observing conforming behavior, but by distinguish-
ing instances of norm conformation from instances
of norm violation (Bicchieri, 2005) and fair and
unfair outcomes (Fehr and Fischbacher, 2004), we
use NCE-based alignment to explicitly contrast val-
idated compromises against inadequate alternatives.
Our experiments show that the approach improved
the quality of smaller LLM-generated compromises
over fine-tuning alone, which only exposes models
to acceptable compromises.
In this paper we present a method that uses em-
pathic neutrality to enhance prompt engineering
to generate compromises. These compromises are
then used, together with poorer quality compro-
mises, to teach an alignment model to align smaller
models. In the following sections, we describe
the different prompt-based models that we inves-
tigated and the automatic and human evaluation
of the generated compromises. We also describe
the method for aligning smaller language models
to generate empathically neutral compromises that
we investigated.

Related work
LLMs excel in academic tasks (GPT-4 achieving
92.1% on MATH) but exhibit limitations in social
intelligence, scoring only 54.4% on SESI bench-
mark (Xu et al., 2024). Similar limitations appear
in interactive gaming contexts, where LLMs per-
form approximately 20% below human baseline
in theory of mind tasks (Liu et al., 2024). Stud-
ies from First-person perspective confirm that de-
spite possessing basic theory of mind capabilities,
LLMs show considerable limitations in managing
complex social interactions compared to human
performance (Hou et al., 2024). Current evalua-
tion methods include traditional psychological as-
sessments like ToMi (Le et al., 2019) and special-
ized datasets such as SocialIQA (Sap et al., 2019),

SocKET (Choi et al., 2023), and SECEU (Wang
et al., 2023). However, newer benchmarks like SO-
TOPIA (Zhou et al., 2024) and EmoBench (Sabour
et al., 2024) face limitations in reflecting real-world
interactions. Prior work generated consensus state-
ments using supervised fine-tuning and re-ranking
(Bakker et al., 2022), or involved humans in se-
lecting common ground (Tessler et al., 2024). We
instead generate multiple compromise suggestions
from open-ended prompts, aiming for balanced
empathy across differing views without human se-
lection or re-ranking.
Synthetic datasets offer a promising solution
for enhancing LLMs’ social capabilities (Ghana-
dian et al., 2024; Hassan et al., 2024; Balog et al.,
2024; Gabriel et al., 2024). These datasets leverage
LLMs’ generative abilities (Dankar and Ibrahim,
2021) while ensuring diverse representation (Ya-
magishi and Nakamura, 2024). Advanced prompt
engineering techniques, particularly using GPT-4
or Claude (Achiam et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2023),
have improved dataset quality (Hikov and Murphy,
2024; Shi et al., 2023). Chain of Thought (CoT)
approaches (Wei et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024; Chu
et al., 2023) show enhanced reasoning capabilities
(Shao et al., 2023), with significant improvements
in specific tasks (Nong et al., 2024). Structured
Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) (Sultan et al., 2024) fur-
ther improves accuracy in document-grounded QA
conversations. Recent development suggest using
parameterized soft prompts instead of traditional
hard-prompting (DeSalvo et al., 2024).
Model alignment with human preferences has
progressed from Reinforcement Learning from Hu-
man Feedback (RLHF) (Kaufmann et al., 2023;
Ouyang et al., 2022) to more efficient alternatives
(Liu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Wang et al.,
2024b). While RLHF aligns models with complex
human values through reward models and policy
optimization (Song et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2023;
Yuan et al., 2024), it remains resource-intensive
and complex (Schulman et al., 2017; Wang et al.,
2024a; Hong et al., 2023). Direct Preference Opti-
mization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2024) simplifies
training by removing the reward model and opti-
mizing the likelihood of preferred responses. Ex-
tensions such as reward model distillation (Fisch
et al., 2024) and KL regularization (Kullback and
Leibler, 1951; Wesego and Rooshenas, 2024; Azar
et al., 2024) further enhance stability. DPOP (Pal
et al., 2024) adds a penalty to maintain preference
alignment with the reference model. InfoNCA and
NCA (Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2010; Chen et al.,
2024) adapt DPO for multi-response settings by
optimizing absolute likelihoods. Finally, methods
like TODO (Guo et al., 2024) and RPO (Yin et al.,
2024) introduce ternary ranking and contrastive
weighting to capture finer-grained preference sig-
nals.
This study focuses on aligning model outputs
in the context of neutral compromise generation.
Prompt engineering is guided by the empathic sim-
ilarity between viewpoints and generated compro-
mise, and this setup is used to generate synthetic
training data. This data is used for fine-tuning and
aligning pretrained LLM to generate these compro-


mises.
3
Compromise Generation using
Empathy-Informed LLM
This section describes the dataset used for our ex-
periments and the generation of candidate compro-
mise sentences through diverse prompt engineering
techniques.
3.1
ContrastingViews Dataset
We adapt the public EmpathyFromPerspectives
dataset Chen et al. (2025) composed of pairs of
contrasting viewpoints by human participants about
feeling safe/less safe and welcome/excluded in pub-
lic spaces (see Appendix C for a summary). Each
pair of viewpoints includes: view_A, which is ei-
ther a safe or welcome viewpoint and a correspond-
ing view_B, which is either a less safe or excluded
viewpoint. Each viewpoint is composed of a place
description, reasons for the viewpoint, and sug-
gested improvements. We randomly selected 1200
safe/less safe and 1200 welcome/excluded pairs for
our generation experiments, and refer to this subset
as the ContrastingViews dataset.
3.2
Empathic similarity model
We adopt the empathic similarity framework
from Shen (2023), which computes an empathic
similarity score sim(fθ(s1), fθ(s2)) between pairs
of stories (s1, s2), where higher scores indicate
greater alignment in empathic content. While Shen
(2023) used Sentence-BERT (Reimers, 2019), we
replace it with the e5-large model (Wang et al.,
2022) for improved sentence representation. To
adapt the similarity model to our scenario, we com-
bined 2,000 annotated story pairs from Shen’s EM-
PATHICSTORIES dataset (Shen, 2023) with 1,000
story pairs from the ContrastingViews dataset.
Prior work (Schopf et al., 2023; Hupkes et al.,
2022) has shown that such pretrained encoders
can support semantic generalization even when ex-
posed to mismatched discourse styles, such as nar-
rative and structured text. The combined dataset
of 3,000 pairs is used to train the similarity model
with a 75/5/20 train/validation/test split. During
inference, this model estimates empathic similarity
between a generated compromise and each of its
corresponding pair of viewpoints.
3.3
LLM generation of compromise data
We aim to generate compromises for each given
pair of positive and negative views for a place. Each
view consists of (i) description of the place (ii) rea-
son of the view (iii) suggestions of improvement.
In order to use all this information as a context for
feeding into an LLM, we follow a prompt template
similar to the Alpaca prompt (Taori et al., 2023).
Recent work suggests that proprietary LLMs excel
at synthetic dataset generation (Cascante-Bonilla
et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2023) with
the help of task specific prompt based strategies,
providing an alternative to human data collection.
We use Claude 3 Opus (Anthropic, 2023) for gen-
erating compromise data.
Using a single compromise as the target con-
strains model generalization capabilities (Gong
et al., 2019). We generated multiple candidate
compromises per view pair, enhancing the model’s
ability to learn diverse resolution patterns. Addi-
tionally, we observed that single prompts were inad-
equate (see section E of the appendix) for our task
as they frequently focus on only one perspective,
which necessitated our exploration of more sophis-
ticated prompt engineering techniques. All three
CoT-based strategies share a common structural
principle designed to promote balance between
the two viewpoints. Each begins by separately ex-
tracting the suggestions from view_A and view_B
before identifying commonalities. This explicit
decomposition ensures that both perspectives are
represented in the model’s reasoning context prior
to compromise generation, preventing the model
from anchoring on one viewpoint, a failure mode
we observed frequently with single prompts (Sec-
tion H). The strategies differ in how they reinforce
this balance using empathic similarityafter initial
generation, as described below.
Chain of Thought (CoT): We initially used CoT
(Chu et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2022) to identify sug-
gestion similarities and derive compromises, as
illustrated in Figure 2. This approach, however,
proved ineffective, the generated text either empha-
sizing a single suggestion too heavily or extending
beyond their intended scope, ultimately leading to
less suitable compromises.
CoT+LLM: LLMs have demonstrated the poten-
tial to refine their outputs through self-generated
feedback, closely aligning with human refinement
techniques (Madaan et al., 2024). In this approach,
we integrated LLM-based self-evaluation scores
(Figure 2). These scores measure empathic simi-
larity between the generated compromise and each
view, ideally achieving high similarity for both
perspectives with minimal discrepancy. Although

3.4
Candidate compromise selection
For each prompting strategy, four compromises are
collected per view pair (resulting in 4 × 4 = 16
compromises per view pair across four prompting
strategies: Single Prompt, CoT, CoT+LLM and
CoT+Feedback). From this set of 16, the top four
responses are selected as candidate compromises
(step 2 in Figure 3) by ranking them according
to an estimate of empathic neutrality (see Table 1).
Neutrality is evaluated using the similarity model to
compute the empathic similarity between the gener-
ated compromise and both view_A and view_B, de-
noted as score_A and score_B, respectively. Then
empathic neutrality is computed as the absolute dif-
ference in empathic similarity |scoreA −scoreB|
In an ideal state of empathic neutrality, the absolute
difference between these scores approaches zero.

4
Human Evaluation of Compromise
Methods
The previous evaluation indicates how well the gen-
erated compromises achieve empirical empathic
neutrality as measured by comparing the empathic
similarity of two opposing viewpoints. We next
conduct a human evaluation.
4.1
Evaluation Methodology
For this, we asked 50 humans to rate compro-
mises generated by the Single Prompt, COT, and
COT+Feedback methods. The participants were
shown pairs of statements about modifications pro-
posed for a place, where one statement was written
by someone who thought positively about the place
and the other statement was written by someone
who felt negatively about the place. Instead of ask-
ing directly how fair a compromise was, which
could be biased by the rater’s personal perspective
and from cognitive priming and carryover effects
of viewing two viewpoints sequentially (Epley and
Gilovich, 2006), a rater was asked to take the view-
point of either the person who felt positively or who
felt negatively for all pairs of statements presented
(assigned viewpoint). The number of raters taking
the positive and negative viewpoints was balanced.
For each pair of statements, raters were asked to
rate on a scale of 1-100 the acceptability of each
of five compromises from their assigned viewpoint.
One of the “compromises” was the positive or neg-
ative statement that they were not to identify with
(‘Opposing View’). The four other compromises
were generated: one by Single Prompt, one by COT,
and two by the COT+Feedback method. Each par-
ticipant rated the compromises for five pairs of
statements, providing ratings from the positive and
negative viewpoints for a total of 100 pairs of state-
ments and 400 generated compromises. For details
about the collection of compromise ratings, see
Appendix D.
4.2
Preference Results
Table 2 shows the percentage of time that each
of the compromise methods was the top choice
(First Preference) and second choice (Second Pref-
erence). We observed that COT+Feedback com-
promises were most preferred (COT+Feedback 1:
37% first, 33% second; COT+Feedback 2: 40%
first, 29% second), outperforming CoT (18%, 24%)
and Single Prompt (5%, 13%). The opposing view
was rarely preferred (0%, 1%).
To verify the statistical robustness of these pref-
erences, we performed three tests on participant
First Preferences: (1) a bootstrap analysis (10,000
iterations) to compute 95% confidence intervals (2)
Wilcoxon signed-rank tests by user to compute the
significance of the different methods against the
Single Prompt method and (3) permutation tests by
on per-item ranks to also compute the significance
of the different methods against the Single Prompt
method. The results shown in Table 3 indicates that
the preference for COT+Feedback is statistically
significant compared to the Single Prompt baseline
(p ≤0.002) for both the Wilcoxon and Permuta-
tion tests. In contrast, the standard COT method
(18%) was not found to be statistically distinguish-

5
Aligning Foundation Models for
Empathically Neutral Compromise
Generation

tion 3 demonstrates that external empathic feed-
back improves compromise quality. However, this
pipeline relies on iterative similarity scoring at in-
ference time, requiring access to both a proprietary
LLM and a trained similarity model. In human
mediation training, practitioners learn to generate
fair proposals not by consulting external fairness
metrics in real time, but by building internal rep-

generation becomes an intrinsic capability rather

Instead of using standard fine-tuning to teach a
model to imitate target outputs, we use an approach
that teaches a model to distinguish good compro-
mises from poor ones. This choice is motivated
by cognitive research on social norm acquisition
showing that humans learn evaluative standards
through contrastive experience, e.g., comparing
norm-conforming behavior against violations (Fehr
and Fischbacher, 2004; Bicchieri, 2005).

This is important
for our task because the model must retain

methods that optimize likelihood ratios, such as
DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024), risk suppressing the
absolute likelihood of even preferred outputs,
degrading generation quality.
5.1
NCE based alignment
We train an NCE model using the candidate com-
promises preferred by human evaluators (Section
4.2) as positive examples to align the model with
verified human social preferences. The negative
examples are the fine-tuned base model’s outputs,
which serve as contrasting cases.
For training efficiency, all parameters are frozen
except the last three layers. Let s_target denote
the sum of log-probabilities that the model assigns
to the tokens of the candidate compromise, and
let s_hypo denote the corresponding sum for the
fine-tuned base model’s own generated output. The
NCE loss (Equation 1) consists of two terms:

Experimental setup on alignment
Datasets: We use the ContrastingViews dataset
together with the synthetic compromises generated
by CoT+Feedback, described in Section 3, to vali-
date our alignment targets. Our smaller models are
trained, when given a pair of opposing views, to
mimic the compromises, whose quality was evalu-
ated by humans in Section 4. Thus our alignment
process optimizes towards a socially valid objec-
tive. The ContrastingViews dataset together with
the genereated compromises were split into training
(75%), development (5%), and test (20%) subsets.
Setup: For all the experiments, we use Llama-
3.1 8B (Dubey et al., 2024) and mistral-7B in-
struct (Jiang et al., 2023) as base models (referred
as Llama and Mistral-7b). We initially fine-tune
the base models for one epoch and use this fine
tuned model for further alignment tasks. We imple-
mented a linear warm-up and cosine decay sched-
uler to dynamically adjust the learning rate with an
initial learning rate of 3e−5. Optimization is per-
formed using the Adam optimizer with β1 = 0.90
and β2 = 0.99. Through empirical tuning, we
found that a weight margin value of 10 was optimal
for task-based loss alignment. We train for 8 and
12 epochs for the NCE-based alignment and task-
loss based alignment, respectively.
Evaluation metrics: We employ a multi-faceted
evaluation strategy: (i) Generation Quality: We
report ROUGE scores (Lin, 2004) to measure se-
mantic alignment with the human-validated candi-
date compromises (see Table 4). (ii) Empathic
Neutrality:
We measure the "neutrality gap"

better balance between viewpoints.

7.1
Quantitative Evaluation
As shown in Table 4, initial generations from pre-

8
Conclusion and Future Work
Our work presents an initial framework for improv-
ing the social intelligence of LLMs for the novel
task of empathically neutral compromise genera-
tion. We propose and conduct human evaluation
of the effectiveness of several prompting strategies,
and show that use of empathic similarity improves
performance. We also show that alignment meth-
ods enable smaller, open-source models (Llama-3.1
8B and Mistral-7B) to approach the compromise
generation quality of Claude 3 Opus, the propri-
etary model used to generate the training data. To
extend this work, we hope to explore socially intel-


ligent tasks beyond place-based conflicts, includ-
ing ethical or policy disagreements, and develop
methods that further maximize empathy toward
both viewpoints. This would help to broaden the
framework’s applicability to real-world mediation
scenarios.

A
Limitations
The COT+feedback approach sought to produce
compromise text that is equally acceptable to both
viewpoints. In the future, we would also like to
include consideration of maximizing the empathy
of each viewpoint to the compromise.
Our collection of compromises was constrained
to keep the data collection required manageable.
The compromises are generated based on two dif-
ferent human viewpoints for a similar type of place.
Although many of the comments about a place ap-
ply generally to a place type, i.e., trails and fencing
in a park, in a real scenario, the expressed view-
points are about the same type of place, rather than
exactly the same. We chose this approach because
collecting compromise data for the same place
would be a much larger undertaking. The prompts
were based on feeling safe/unsafe or welcome/ex-
cluded. Generalization to other prompts was not
done because this would have also increased the
required size of the negative viewpoints. These
generalizations are left for future work.
While this place based focus on safety and inclu-
sivity enables a controlled exploration of empathy-
neutral compromises, it inherently limits the frame-
work’s immediate generalization to broader real-
world scenarios, such as interpersonal conflicts,
policy debates, or collaborative decision-making
in non-spatial domains (i.e., ethical dilemmas in
team projects or ideological disagreements in com-
munity forums). The reliance on physical "places"
as the locus of conflict may overlook nuances in
abstract or multifaceted disputes, potentially reduc-
ing the framework’s utility for diverse mediation
contexts where viewpoints diverge on intangible
issues.
To enhance generalizability, future work could
expand the dataset to include contrasting view-
points on non-place-based topics, such as political
policies (i.e., environmental regulations) or social
norms (i.e., workplace diversity initiatives), by scal-
ing negative viewpoint collection through crowd-
sourcing platforms or synthetic augmentation tech-
niques. This would test the framework’s robustness
across domains, potentially incorporating multi-
turn dialogues to simulate ongoing negotiations.
While our neutrality metric captures empathic
balance, it does not account for societal biases (i.e.,
race, gender, class) present in inputs or LLM gen-
erations. LLMs may overlook power asymmetries
or ethical subtleties due to limited social reasoning.
Moreover, the dataset’s narrow domain limits gen-
eralizability. Future work should explicitly evaluate
and mitigate such biases.
The Human Study comparing different compro-
mise generation texts presented only a sample of
4 of the generated texts per viewpoint pair, rather
than all 16, because humans would have difficulty
rating all items reliably.
B
Ethical Considerations
Our goal in this work was to generate compromises
that are equally acceptable to the two parties with
different viewpoints. Similar to the general dangers
of some people trusting all results generated by
an LLM, the generated compromises should be
viewed as suggestions for discussion areas, rather
than a compromise that each person should agree
to.
Our work is a first step . In the future, it should
be used as an aid rather than being relied upon
directly. However, a possible future misuse is in
sensitive conflict scenarios, where the compromises
are not used as suggestions but instead as direct
solutions. This is a societal problem, similar to
other issues that generative AI has created, such as
the generation of fake videos of real people and the
generation of mental health advice.
C
Summary of Dataset Collection
Method in Chen et al. (2025)
We briefly summary the data collection method
used by Chen et al. (2025), which provided the
contrasting viewpoints used in our work. As shown
in Figure 5, in stage 1 (upper row), participants
recruited from dscout1 provide views (view_B)
about places where they felt less safe/excluded.
For each place, they explained their feelings and
suggested modifications to improve safety or in-
clusivity. Place descriptions for less safe/excluded
places were each grouped into 14 clusters using ag-
glomerative clustering. A classifier was developed
to match new views to these clusters.
In stage 2 (bottom row), new participants from
Prolific 2 wrote views (view_A) about places where
they felt safe/welcome. The classifier matched each
view_A to a view_B from the place-type cluster
corresponding to view_A.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel academ- ically but struggle with social intelligence tasks, such as creating good compromises. In this paper, we present methods for generating em- pathically neutral compromises between two opposing viewpoints. We first compared four different prompt engineering methods using Claude 3 Opus and a dataset of 2,400 contrast- ing views on shared places. A subset of the gen- erated compromises was evaluated for accept- ability in a 50-participant study. We found that the best method for generating compromises between two views used external empathic sim- ilarity between a compromise and each view- point as iterative feedback, outperforming stan- dard Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning. The results indicate that the use of empathic neutral- ity improves the acceptability of compromises. The dataset of generated compromises was then used to train two smaller foundation models via margin-based alignment of human preferences, improving efficiency and removing the need for empathy estimation during inference.
